headline: Captree dock talk: the ocean's a mess, but the bay's doing the heavy lifting
subhead: With swell hammering the beach, the smart money this week is inside the inlet and up in Great South Bay, where warm water pouring out on the ebb is stacking bass, fluke, and a few stray weakfish along the current seams.
body_markdown:
Ran into a guy at the Captree bait shop Tuesday morning loading a cooler he clearly hadn't filled yet, grumbling about getting bounced around off Democrat Point the evening before. Said he never even got a bucktail to the bottom clean — the swell kept walking his boat off the drift. I told him what I've been telling everybody this week: leave the ocean alone for a few days and go fish the bay like your father did. He didn't love hearing it, but he went home and came back Wednesday with better stories.

Here's the honest read. The Bight buoy off the coast is showing better than three and a half feet of swell on a short six-second period, which is a sloppy, disorganized sea — not the kind of water that lets you work a bucktail or a plug with any confidence off the outer bars or the Robert Moses jetties. Surface temp out there is sitting near 76, which on paper sounds great for albies and bonito showing up on bait balls — and we flagged that watch last week when the water first pushed past 70. But nothing's confirmed it yet. No bait balls reported, no surface action off the outer bars. Keep an eye on it, because that temperature trend hasn't reversed, but I wouldn't plan a trip around it just yet.

What's actually paying off is inside. The bay's running noticeably warmer than the open Atlantic right now, and that thermal gap is exactly why the fishing has funneled into the inlet and up into Great South Bay itself. Every ebb tide, that warm, bait-rich water gets squeezed out through Fire Island Inlet, and everything that eats gets stacked along the current seams where the bay water meets the harder ocean flow. That's your money window — the back half of the outgoing, when the seam sharpens up and you can see the color change right off the Democrat Point rip.

Striped bass have been working that seam in fits and starts. Nothing's been a blitz, but there've been enough fish moving through on bunker and peanut bunker to make it worth a few drifts with bucktails — 1 to 1.5-ounce white or bubblegum, bounced slow along the bottom edge of the rip where the depth drops from eight feet to fifteen. If you see any surface disturbance or diving birds working bait pushed tight to the beach near the point, that's worth a cast with a topwater plug before you go back to bouncing bucktails. Bunker schools have been thick enough elsewhere on the coast this summer that when they do funnel into the inlet, things can get loud fast — so it pays to have a popper rigged and ready even while you're jigging.

Fluke are still very much a bay fish right now, and the Robert Moses bridge pilings remain the most consistent stop on the map. Twenty-five to thirty-five feet of water on the outgoing, drifting slow with white Gulp Swimming Mullets on three-quarter-ounce bucktails, tipped with a strip of squid for insurance. Sizes have been mixed — plenty of shorts mixed in with keepers in the 18 to 22-inch range, so it's a pick-through-them kind of bite rather than a limit-fast morning. Worth working both sides of the bridge on the same tide, since current speed and depth shift noticeably between the east and west spans.

Weakfish have been scarce, which isn't new for this stretch of the bay in August, but there've been a few legal fish coming out of the deeper holes off Patchogue and Sayville at dusk, taken on bucktails tipped with squid strips fished slow along bottom. Not a pattern to build a trip around, but if you're already out there working the last of the light, it's worth a few extra drifts through the deeper channel bends.

Porgies are doing exactly what they're supposed to do in August — stacked on the bay-side structure inside the inlet, hungry, and forgiving. Small hooks, sandworms or clam, standard high-low rigs over any of the rockier patches inside the inlet mouth. Good action for anyone bringing kids or just wanting a bucket of dinner without overthinking the tide.

One piece of real news worth passing along: Heckscher State Park's Field 6 is running its first-season night fishing trial this summer, Friday through Sunday, dusk to dawn, through Labor Day. That's a legitimate new look at the north shore of Great South Bay after dark, and it lines up nicely with everything we've been talking about — warm bay water pouring out on the ebb, bass working the channel edges under cover of darkness. You'll need a Night Sport Fishing Permit or 4x4 permit on the dash, and access is Field 6 only, but for anyone who's wanted a crack at those bay-side channel bends at night without trespassing on private bulkheads, this is the opening. Bunker chunks or a live eel fished tight to the channel drop-off on the outgoing looks like the play.

Looking ahead, if that ocean swell settles down even a little by the weekend, I'd give the outer bars a look for the first sign of albies or bonito working bait — the water's warm enough and the setup's been building for a couple weeks now. But until the sea state cooperates, the bay is where the paychecks are. Fish the ebb, work the seams, and don't be afraid to put in the time on the fluke drift even when the fish are running small — the keepers are mixed in, you just have to pick through them.
